name: Amiga 500
notes: An example of a computer. Edit it, copy it, or remove it once you have your own.

name: Sega Master System
notes: An example of a console. It records no storage, so that box never appears.

name: Game Boy
notes: An example of a handheld.

name: Generic 486 PC
notes: An example of a PC. Real board models are better recorded one at a time.

name: Amiga 2000
notes: The desktop Amiga with Zorro II slots. The first one an expansion card was designed for.

fields.label: Expansion
fields.value: Zorro II, plus ISA and a CPU slot

name: Amiga 3000
notes: 32-bit Zorro III, SCSI on the board.

slots.notes: Zorro III, backwards compatible with Zorro II
Zorro II cards work in the same slots

name: Amiga 4000
notes: AGA and Zorro III. Shipped with a 68040 or a 68EC030 depending on the model.

slots.notes: Zorro III, backwards compatible with Zorro II
Zorro II cards work in the same slots

name: PET 2001
notes: The first one. Calculator keyboard and a built-in cassette deck.

name: CBM 4032
notes: 40-column PET with the full keyboard and BASIC 4.0.

name: CBM 8032
notes: The 80-column business machine. What most European offices meant by a PET.

name: VIC-20
notes: The first computer of any kind to sell a million. 5 KB, and most of it spoken for.

name: Commodore 64
notes: The breadbin. The best-selling computer model of all time, and the reason half this catalogue exists.

name: Commodore 64C
notes: The restyled C64 in the flatter case, usually with the 8580 SID - which is why a C64C and a breadbin do not sound quite alike.

name: SX-64
notes: The portable C64, with a 5" colour screen and a 1541 built in. Portable in the sense that it has a handle.

name: Commodore 128
notes: Three machines in one case: native 128 mode, a genuine C64 mode, and CP/M on a second processor.

name: Commodore 128D
notes: The 128 in a desktop case with the 1571 built in and a detachable keyboard.

name: Commodore 16
notes: The 264 series in a breadbin case. Not C64 compatible, which is most of what anybody remembers about it.

name: Plus/4
notes: 64 KB and four applications in ROM. The productivity machine nobody had asked for.

name: Amiga 1000
notes: The first one, with Kickstart loaded from floppy at every boot and the developers' signatures moulded into the case.

fields.label: Memory
fields.value: 256 KB, 512 KB with the front expansion

name: Amiga 500+
notes: An A500 with ECS, Kickstart 2.04 and a battery on the board - which is worth checking before you plug one in.

name: Amiga 600
notes: The small one, with PCMCIA and room for a 2.5" drive, and no numeric keypad.

name: Amiga 1200
notes: AGA in a wedge. The one most people mean when they say they still have an Amiga.

name: Amiga 3000T
notes: The tower 3000, with more Zorro slots than anybody filled.

slots.notes: Zorro II cards work in the same slots

name: Amiga 4000T
notes: The tower 4000. The last Amiga Commodore shipped before it stopped shipping anything.

slots.notes: Zorro II cards work in the same slots

name: CDTV
notes: An A500 in a black hi-fi case with a CD drive, sold to people who did not want a computer. They did not want this either.

name: Amiga CD32
notes: An A1200 without the keyboard, and the first 32-bit CD console anywhere. Commodore went under four months later.

slots.notes: rear expansion connector, for the MPEG and SX-1 modules

name: NES (front loader)
notes: The front-loading NES. The loading mechanism is the thing that fails, and the reason so many need the pins reseating.

name: NES (top loader)
notes: The later top loader. No lockout chip and no rotting pin connector, but composite out was dropped for RF.

name: Super Nintendo
notes: Mode 7 and the S-SMP sound chip. The PAL machine runs at 50 Hz and it shows.

name: Nintendo 64
notes: Four controller ports as standard, which is most of what people remember about it.

fields.label: Memory
fields.value: 4 MB RDRAM, 8 MB with the Expansion Pak

name: Mega Drive (model 1)
notes: The one with the headphone socket and the better sound. Genesis in North America.

name: Mega Drive (model 2)
notes: Smaller, cheaper, no headphone socket, and mono unless you take stereo from the AV port.

name: Mega-CD (model 2)
notes: A CD drive, a second 68000 and a scaling chip, sat under a Mega Drive.

fields.label: Memory
fields.value: 6 MB total across the two machines

slots.notes: the Mega Drive sits on top

name: Sega Saturn
notes: Two SH-2s and a reputation for being hard to write for. The PAL machine came late and thin on titles.

name: Dreamcast
notes: GD-ROM, a modem in the box, and the last console Sega made.

name: Master System II
notes: Cheaper, smaller, no card slot and no reset button. Alex Kidd is built in.

name: PlayStation (SCPH-1002)
notes: The early PAL machine, with the parallel port on the back that later revisions dropped.

name: Atari 2600 VCS
notes: Woodgrain and six switches. The machine that made a cartridge a thing you bought.

name: Atari 7800
notes: Plays 2600 cartridges as well, which almost nothing else of its generation could say.

name: Neo Geo AES
notes: The arcade board in a home case, and cartridges that cost as much as a console.

name: PC Engine (white)
notes: HuCards the size of a credit card, and the smallest console anybody had made.

slots.notes: expansion bus, for the CD-ROM unit

name: Intellivision
notes: Disc controllers with a keypad, and overlays that slid in over them.

slots.notes: hand controllers, hard-wired on early units

name: ColecoVision
notes: The expansion module let it play 2600 cartridges, which Atari went to court about.

name: Vectrex
notes: Its own vector monitor built in, so it never needed a television and never looked like anything else.

name: 3DO FZ-1
notes: Panasonic's build of a standard other people were meant to licence. Almost nobody did.

name: Atari Jaguar
notes: Sold as 64-bit, which was true of two of the chips and an argument about the rest.

fields.label: Processor
fields.value: Motorola 68000 @ 13.3 MHz with Tom and Jerry

slots.notes: expansion port, for the CD unit

name: Philips CD-i 910
notes: Sold as an interactive appliance rather than a console, which is why it is shaped like a video recorder.

slots.notes: expansion bay, for the Digital Video cartridge

name: Game Boy Pocket
notes: Smaller, two AAAs instead of four AAs, and a screen you can actually read.

name: Game Boy Color
notes: Backwards compatible, and the colour palette it applies to old cartridges is chosen by a key combination at boot.

name: Game Boy Advance
notes: No backlight, which is the entire reason the SP exists.

name: Game Gear
notes: A backlit Master System that ate six AA batteries in four hours. The capacitors have all failed by now.

name: Atari Lynx II
notes: Colour, backlit and left-handed if you wanted, three years before anybody else managed the first two.

name: WonderSwan Color
notes: Held either way up, and it ran for thirty hours on one AA. Japan only.

name: ZX Spectrum 48K
notes: Rubber keys and colour clash. The machine most British bedrooms learned to program on.

name: ZX Spectrum +2
notes: Amstrad's Spectrum, with the tape deck built in and an AY chip that made the music worth listening to.

name: Atari 520ST
notes: MIDI in and out as standard, which is why so many studios still have one.

name: Atari 1040STF
notes: A megabyte and the floppy drive inside the case. The one most people had.

name: Atari Mega ST
notes: Detached keyboard, a blitter and an internal bus, sold at people who did work on it.

name: Amstrad CPC 464
notes: Sold with its own monitor, which powered the machine — so a dead monitor is a dead computer.

name: Amstrad CPC 6128
notes: 128 KB and a 3-inch disk drive, in the format only Amstrad ever really used.

name: MSX2
notes: A standard rather than a machine, so a Sony and a Philips run the same cartridges.

name: Apple IIe
notes: Seven expansion slots and a machine that stayed on sale for eleven years.

fields.label: Memory
fields.value: 64 KB, 128 KB with the auxiliary card

name: BBC Micro Model B
notes: The school computer, with more ports on the back than anything else of its size.

name: Acorn Electron
notes: The cut-down BBC. One chip did most of it, and it was slower for the same reason it was cheaper.

name: Acorn A3000
notes: ARM in a home computer, six years before anybody was putting it in a telephone.

name: Atari 800XL
notes: ANTIC and GTIA doing display lists, years before anyone called it a graphics chip.

name: Atari 130XE
notes: 128 KB, bank switched, in the flatter case that matched the ST.

name: Macintosh Plus
notes: SCSI and a megabyte, and the first Mac you could sensibly expand.

name: Sharp X68000 EXPERT
notes: An arcade board Sharp sold as a home computer, in a case shaped like two towers.

name: NEC PC-9801VX
notes: The Japanese office standard for a decade, and nothing like a PC inside.

name: TRS-80 Model I
notes: Sold in a high street chain, which is most of why it sold at all.

name: Dragon 32
notes: Built in Wales, near enough a CoCo, and incompatible with everything British around it.

name: Oric Atmos
notes: The Oric-1 with a keyboard you could type on, which was the complaint it was built to answer.

name: SAM Coupé
notes: A Spectrum successor that arrived after everyone had bought an Amiga.

name: Sinclair QL
notes: Microdrives, a 68008, and a launch so early the first machines shipped with a ROM hanging out of the back.

name: ZX81
notes: One kilobyte, a membrane keyboard, and a RAM pack that fell off if you breathed on it.

fields.label: Memory
fields.value: 1 KB, 16 KB with the RAM pack

name: Luxor ABC 80
notes: The Swedish school computer, on an ABC bus and speaking BASIC in Swedish error messages.
